title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Two Data Types

Vector data represent discrete features with coordinates: points (nest sites, camera stations), lines (streams, roads, GPS tracks), polygons (home ranges, park boundaries, watersheds). Handled by sf, class sf / sfc.
Raster data represent a continuous surface as a regular grid of cells: elevation, canopy cover, temperature, predicted density. Handled by terra, class SpatRaster.
terra also carries its own vector class, SpatVector, so raster and vector operations can talk to each other without leaving the package.








Coordinate reference systems


A CRS tells R where on Earth your coordinates sit and what the units mean. Layers must share a CRS before you overlay, clip, or measure. Mismatched CRS is the single most common source of silent spatial errors.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Setup for This Section
The raster examples reuse the three vector layers built in the previous section. If you jumped straight here, or refreshed the page, run this cell first to recreate them.

library(sf)
set.seed(591)

n <- 25
stations <- sf::st_as_sf(
  data.frame(site_id  = sprintf("S%02d", 1:n),
             easting  = runif(n, 280500, 291500),
             northing = runif(n, 5180500, 5191500),
             effort   = sample(20:60, n, replace = TRUE)),
  coords = c("easting", "northing"), crs = 32612)

reserve <- st_sf(name = "Wilderness Unit",
  geometry = st_sfc(st_polygon(list(matrix(
    c(282000, 5182000, 289000, 5182500, 290000, 5188000,
      283500, 5190000, 282000, 5182000), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE))), crs = 32612))

stream <- sf::st_sf(name = "Lost Creek",
                    geometry = sf::st_sfc(sf::st_linestring(matrix(
                      c(280500, 5183000, 284000, 5185500,
                        287500, 5186500, 291500, 5190000), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)), crs = 32612))

c(stations = nrow(stations), reserve = nrow(reserve), stream = nrow(stream))

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Simulating an Elevation Surface

library(terra)

set.seed(591)

elev <- terra::rast(nrows = 60, 
                    ncols = 60,
                    xmin = 280000,
                    xmax = 292000,
                    ymin = 5180000,
                    ymax = 5192000,
                    crs  = "EPSG:32612")

# Two Gaussian ridges plus noise
xy <- terra::xyFromCell(elev, 1:ncell(elev))
d1 <- sqrt((xy[, 1] - 284000)^2 + (xy[, 2] - 5189000)^2)
d2 <- sqrt((xy[, 1] - 289500)^2 + (xy[, 2] - 5183000)^2)

values(elev) <- 1300 +
  900 * exp(-(d1 / 3200)^2) +
  600 * exp(-(d2 / 2600)^2) +
  rnorm(ncell(elev), 0, 30)

names(elev) <- "elev_m"
elev







Note


rast() defines the grid geometry, i.e., extent, resolution, and CRS before any values exist. values()<- fills the cells row by row from the top-left. res(elev) confirms each cell is 200 × 200 m.

section: Map Algebra and a Raster Stack
text:
Map Algebra and a Raster Stack
Rasters behave like numbers — you can add, multiply, and threshold them directly.

set.seed(591)

noise <- terra::rast(elev)                     # empty raster, same grid
values(noise) <- rnorm(terra::ncell(elev), 0, 6)

# Canopy declines with elevation, then is clipped to 0-100%
canopy <- terra::clamp(95 - 0.045 * (elev - 1300) + noise, 0, 100)
names(canopy) <- "canopy_pct"

# Distance from every cell to the stream
stream_v <- terra::vect(stream)
dist_str <- terra::distance(terra::rast(elev), stream_v)
names(dist_str) <- "dist_stream_m"

covs <- c(elev, canopy, dist_str)
covs

plot(covs, col = hcl.colors(50, "Viridis"), nc = 3)

Three panels: elevation, canopy cover, and distance to the stream. All three share the same grid, so they can be stacked and used together.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Neighbourhoods and Terrain

# 5 x 5 moving-window mean removes the simulated noise
elev_smooth <- terra::focal(elev, w = matrix(1, 5, 5), fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
names(elev_smooth) <- "elev_smooth"

slope <- terra::terrain(elev_smooth, v = "slope", unit = "degrees")

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(elev_smooth, col = terrain.colors(50), main = "Smoothed elevation (m)")
plot(slope, col = hcl.colors(50, "Inferno"), main = "Slope (degrees)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Smoothing removes the pixel-level noise so terrain() returns a realistic slope surface. Steepest values ring the flanks of each ridge; the summits and the valley floor are flat.






Note


focal() is the workhorse for scale questions: change the window size and you change the grain at which a covariate is measured, which often matters more to a habitat model than the covariate itself.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Reclassifying into Categories

rcl <- matrix(c(   0, 1500, 1,
                1500, 1900, 2,
                1900, 5000, 3),
              ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)

bands <- terra::classify(elev, rcl, include.lowest = TRUE)
levels(bands) <- data.frame(id   = 1:3,
                            band = c("Valley (<1500 m)",
                                     "Montane (1500-1900 m)",
                                     "Subalpine (>1900 m)"))

terra::freq(bands)

plot(bands,
     col = c("#EFE8D4", "#DFD1A7", "#70002E"),
     main = "Elevation bands")

freq() reports the cell count in each band, and each cell is 200 × 200 m, so multiplying by 0.04 converts directly to km².

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Cropping, Masking, and Resampling

reserve_v <- terra::vect(reserve)

elev_res <- terra::mask(terra::crop(elev, reserve_v), reserve_v)

# Coarsen from 200 m to 800 m cells
elev_coarse <- terra::aggregate(elev, fact = 4, fun = mean)

res(elev)
res(elev_coarse)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(elev_res, col = terrain.colors(50), main = "Clipped to wilderness unit")
plot(terra::vect(reserve), add = TRUE, border = "#1D3C34", lwd = 2)
plot(elev_coarse, col = terrain.colors(50), main = "Aggregated to 800 m cells")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

crop() cuts the extent down to the polygon’s bounding box; mask() then sets everything outside the polygon itself to NA. You almost always want both.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Reprojecting a Raster

elev_ll <- terra::project(elev, "EPSG:4326")

terra::crs(elev_ll, describe = TRUE)$name
round(as.vector(terra::ext(elev_ll)), 4)
round(terra::res(elev_ll), 6)          # now in degrees, not metres

plot(elev_ll,
     col = terrain.colors(50),
     main = "Elevation in longitude and latitude")







Important


Reprojecting a raster resamples it: cell values are interpolated onto a new grid, so the result is not identical to the original. Reproject vectors when you can and rasters only when you must, and use method = "near" for categorical rasters so classes are not averaged into nonsense.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Extracting Raster Values at Points

station_covs <- terra::extract(covs, terra::vect(stations), ID = FALSE)

site_data <- cbind(sf::st_drop_geometry(stations)["site_id"], station_covs)
head(site_data)

# Covariates are correlated - always check before modelling
round(cor(site_data[, c("elev_m", "canopy_pct", "dist_stream_m")]), 2)

pairs(site_data[, c("elev_m", "canopy_pct", "dist_stream_m")],
      pch = 19,
      col = "#70002E")

Elevation and canopy cover are strongly negatively correlated by construction, which is exactly the collinearity you would flag before fitting a model with both.

Writing and Reading Rasters

terra::writeRaster(elev, "elev.tif", overwrite = TRUE)
list.files(pattern = "tif")

elev2 <- terra::rast("elev.tif")
elev2

all.equal(terra::global(elev, "mean")[1, 1], terra::global(elev2, "mean")[1, 1])







Note


GeoTIFF stores the values, the grid, and the CRS in one file. For a multi-layer stack, writeRaster() writes all layers as bands. That is a good reason to name them first.

text:
Your Turn: Raster Analysis







Exercise 7


This mask keeps cells below 1,800 m and above 40% canopy cover. Run it, then change either threshold, or swap & for |, and watch the proportion change.





library(terra)
set.seed(591)
elev <- terra::rast(nrows = 60,
                    ncols = 60,
                    xmin = 280000,
                    xmax = 292000,
                    ymin = 5180000,
                    ymax = 5192000, 
                    crs = "EPSG:32612")
xy <- terra::xyFromCell(elev, 1 : terra::ncell(elev))
d1 <- sqrt((xy[, 1] - 284000)^2 + (xy[, 2] - 5189000)^2)
d2 <- sqrt((xy[, 1] - 289500)^2 + (xy[, 2] - 5183000)^2)
values(elev) <- 1300 + 900 * exp(-(d1 / 3200)^2) +
  600 * exp(-(d2 / 2600)^2) + rnorm(terra::ncell(elev), 0, 30)
names(elev) <- "elev_m"
noise <- terra::rast(elev); terra::values(noise) <- rnorm(terra::ncell(elev), 0, 6)
canopy <- terra::clamp(95 - 0.045 * (elev - 1300) + noise, 0, 100)
names(canopy) <- "canopy_pct"

# Logical rasters can be combined with & and |
suitable <- (elev < 1800) & (canopy > 40)
names(suitable) <- "suitable"

# Proportion of cells that qualify
global(suitable, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE)

plot(suitable, col = c("#EFE8D4", "#1D3C34"), main = "Suitable habitat (green)")








Hint


Canopy cover is stored as a percentage from 0 to 100, so “more than 40%” is canopy > 40. A logical raster holds 0s and 1s, so its mean is the proportion of TRUE cells.











Solution


1suitable <- (elev < 1800) & (canopy > 40)
names(suitable) <- "suitable"

2terra::global(suitable, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE)
3freq(suitable)

1

& combines them cell by cell.

2

The mean of a 0/1 raster is the proportion of cells that qualify.

3

freq() gives the raw cell counts. Multiply by 0.04 for km², since cells are 200 × 200 m.

Ask up front: “How many of you have data with xy coordinates?” Almost every hand goes up. Why do you think your data includes that information?
Space is not just a passive background; it is an active player that shapes interactions, dispersal, and evolutionary trajectories.
This lesson is a gentle introduction to the role of space and trajectory of incorporating space into ecology.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Tobler’s First Law of Geography

“Everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things.”

This means that samples from nearby locations are more similar than samples far apart.

The first spatial concept is what is known as Tobler’s first law of geography.
In this class, but more broadly in spatial ecology we borrow a lot from geography.
This statement means that geography is never random. If you sample two points close to each other, they are likely to be similar simply because of their proximity. Your favorite cafe is likely to be the same as your neighbors cafe and less likely to be the same as MSU students living in Bozeman.
Fun fact about Tobler is that he was a cartographer and statistician published the first paper on using computers for making maps.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Space: the final frontier

Kareiva opened a 1994 Ecology editorial by calling space the final frontier for ecological theory.

Ecology had been about space (e.g., Darwin’s entangled bank and Hutchinson’s ecological theater).

What changed in the 1990s was not the recognition that space matters. It was the arrival of data that were spatially explicit and models that could use them.


In ecology, space has been called the final frontier.
This is what Kareiva wrote in 1994 in a one-page Ecology editorial piece “Space: the final frontier for ecological theory”.
Darwin’s entangled bank: Plants, bugs, birds, and worms depend on each other and compete for survival in a shared space. The “entangled bank” is the famous final-paragraph metaphor in Charles Darwin’s On the Origin of Species.
Likewise, Hutchinson’s ecological theatre refers to habitat/space limits as a driving force for species dynamics.
Kareiva’s phrase is a Star Trek reference and if you are under 30 you might miss it. The joke is that it arrived 40-ish years later.
The point is that spatial ecology was not a conceptual breakthrough. It was overwhelmingly a data-and-computation breakthrough applied to concepts that Watt had articulated in 1947. The field simply had not built the tools to say so quantitatively.
new methods in this field usually follow new data, not new theory.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Spatial ecology

“The study and modeling of the role(s) of space on ecological processes, which in turn affect ecological patterns.”

Definition by Fletcher & Fortin, 2018



The term was coined by Tilman and Kareiva in 1997, in an edited volume on the role of space in population dynamics and interspecific interactions.
“spatial ecology” is younger than most of your students. The field naming itself in 1997 is recent enough that the founding figures are still publishing

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Processes and patterns
We usually observe the pattern and want to infer the process.

Space acts on processes (dispersal, competition, demography)
Processes generate patterns (distributions, abundance surfaces)
process → pattern → inference



space acts on processes, and processes generate patterns. The arrow runs process to pattern.

Almost everything we do analytically runs the arrow backwards — we observe pattern and try to infer process. Many processes can generate the same pattern.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Space in Ecology: dependence

All aspects of ecology play out in space.

If space is inherent to every ecological process, then any analysis that assumes observations are independent and identically located is making a claim about biology which is usually false.

In ecology, we know that space is inherent to every ecol process. This is one sentence to hang the semester on.
If you find a Wood Turtle in a specific stream reach, the odds of finding another one ten meters away are much higher than finding one ten kilometers away. This is Tobler’s Law.
In statistics, this creates a “nuisance” because if our samples aren’t independent, we are essentially “double-counting” our data, which makes our results look more significant than they really are
Would that be a type I or type II error? False positives

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Space in Ecology: scale

All aspects of ecology play out in space.

Spatial structure can alter outcomes of ecological studies.

Ignoring space isn’t a neutral simplification, it’s rather an assumption that location carries no information. Almost nobody would defend that claim out loud, yet it’s baked into most standard models.
Consider the Wood Turtle: it needs instream habitat for winter, riparian areas for spring, and upland sites for summer foraging. It operates across an entire watershed mosaic. If we only study the turtle at the “microhabitat” scale (the logs it sits on), we miss the “landscape” scale (the connectivity between the river and the forest) that it needs to survive its 50+ year lifespan

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Space-environment relationship
SA-env: Spatial structure of the environment
SD: Spatial dependence of species response to spatially structured environment
SA-sp: Spatial autocorrelation of the species

Space affects species patterns directly and indirectly. Let’s talk about this arrow. SD — spatial dependence: This is the arrow ecologists usually want to estimate. It is the habitat association, the resource selection coefficient, the niche relationship.
The problem: SD is measured in a system where SA-env and SA-sp are both operating, and all three arrows produce the same patterns.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Spatial pattern: SA-env
SA-env: Spatial structure of the environment

SA-env is a property of the world, not of the sampling or the species.


-SA-env : The environment is autocorrelated for reasons that have nothing to do with your study organism. Elevation is smooth. Temperature is smooth. Soil type comes in patches because geology comes in patches.
Nearby places resemble each other environmentally, and that would be true if your species went extinct tomorrow.
what’s the coldest place within 200 m of where you are sitting? The U.S. Forest Service building just off East Beckwith Avenue or Mansfield Library.
what’s the coldest place within 200 km of where you are sitting? Glacier NP, Lost Trail Pass near Idaho border,
The first is nearly the same temperature as the room; the second could be 20°C different.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Spatial pattern: SA-sp
SA-sp: Spatial autocorrelation of the species

Organisms cluster for endogenous reasons: limited dispersal, territoriality, conspecific attraction, contagious reproduction, local demographic history.


-SA-sp: Organisms cluster for endogenous reasons: limited dispersal, territoriality, conspecific attraction, contagious reproduction, local demographic history.
This is the arrow that would still exist in a perfectly uniform environment.
“so how do you ever separate them?” with difficulty, with assumptions, and sometimes not at all — which is why experiments like Huffaker’s, coming up in three slides, retain their value.
Exogenous processes are organism responses to environmental factors that are themselves spatially structured. Climate, local habitat features, microhabitat heterogeneity, patch disturbance and succession
Endogenous processes - Movement, dispersal, migration - Demography, genetic variation, behavior - Competition, facilitation, trophic interactions

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Why does it matter?
All three produce similar maps, confusing them has direct costs:

False positive error. Autocorrelated residuals violate independence; standard errors shrink, p-values shrink, and you discover relationships that are not there.
Wrong mechanism. You attribute to habitat what dispersal produced, or vice versa.
Bad extrapolation. A model fitted to a confounded signal predicts badly in a new landscape.


Autocorrelation means your effective sample size is smaller than your nominal sample size, sometimes by an order of magnitude.
Give the concrete version: 500 vegetation plots on a 30 m grid may carry the information of perhaps 40 independent plots. Everything downstream of that mistake is wrong in the same direction — too confident.

Print slide 60 on cardstock and cut into 11 cards; one set per pair, so a class of 30 needs 15 sets. They laminate well and you will reuse them every year.
Deliberately place three labelled zones on tables rather than having students write answers. Physically moving a card is a commitment, and commitments generate the arguments you want to overhear while circulating.
Do not answer questions during phase 1. Write recurring ones on the board and address them in phase 3.
preparation:

Card 10 is the trap and it is the most valuable card in the set. It is not biological aggregation at all — it is double-counting, a measurement artefact that produces a signature identical to SA-sp.
Most pairs file it under SA-sp, which is defensible and gives you the opening to make the point that the same pattern in data can arise from biology or from sampling design, and the data cannot tell you which. That is the honest version of what Chapter 5 does and does not deliver.
Card 6 is the second-best card: a legacy effect masquerading as an environmental gradient.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Theoretical Foundations

Traditionally, ecological models ignored the role of space (e.g., classic Lotka-Volterra models).
However, spatial structure can fundamentally alter outcomes:

Facilitates species coexistence by creating spatial refuges
Generates source-sink dynamics where sink habitats are sustained by immigration
Drives spatial population synchrony through regional climatic factors or dispersal



Ecological theory has undergone a paradigm shift. We now understand that ignoring space can lead to completely wrong conclusions. For example, two competing species that cannot coexist in a well-mixed laboratory beaker can easily coexist in a spatially heterogeneous environment where they use different spatial niches.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text: Spatial Ecology Timeline

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Plant community: Watt 1947

Pattern and process are linked, not separate objects of study.



This is a bunchgrass slope outside town. Is anything happening in this picture? Most people say no. It looks like a still life. Watt’s answer was that you’re looking at a time-lapse that someone has flattened into a single frame — and once you learn to read it, the picture starts moving.
Think about a family reunion photo. In one photo you have a newborn, a teenager, a parent, a grandparent. You are not looking at four unrelated people. You are looking at one human life cycle displayed all at once in space. Watt’s insight was that a plant community does the same thing: the patch dying back over there and the patch filling in over here are not different communities. They’re the same community at different points in its rotation.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Pattern and Process

A static plant community is in fact a dynamic mosaic of patches rotating through life and death.


Plants occur in bounded communities, i.e., patches, that together form a dynamic mosaic across the landscape.
Patterns arise from processes such as competition and dispersal.


As analogy, think about the difference bet escalator vs. carousel. Back in a day, the dominant idea was that succession runs one direction and stops at the top like an escalator. Watt gave it a carousel: every horse is going around, they’re all at different points, and the ride as a whole never ends. Neither horse is “ahead.”
A plant community that looks static is actually a slow-motion mosaic. Every patch within it is somewhere in a life cycle — being born, filling in, peaking, falling apart — and because the patches are out of step with one another, the whole holds still while every part of it churns.
the landscape as a whole is stable: stadium analogy

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Universe of oranges: Huffaker 1958
Lotka-Volterra models assume every predator can encounter every prey with equal probability.



Lotka-Volterra assumes every predator can encounter every prey with equal probability, which is a statement that space does not exist.
This mathematical model was difficult to reproduce in the lab.

In small, homogeneous habitats: predator eats prey, both crash. No stability.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Spatial refugia

Space can stabilise an interaction that is unstable without it.

The physical layout of the landscape, i.e., spatial configuration, is what prevents total collapse or accelerates colonizations.

Huffaker worked with predatory and herbivorous mites on arrays of oranges, manipulating the spatial structure of the arena.

With spatial refugia for prey and barriers slowing the predator: persistent oscillations. The system holds.

Same species. Same biology. Different spatial structure, different outcome.
Huffaker built elaborate arrays of oranges with vaseline barriers and wooden posts so the prey mite could disperse by silk and the predator couldn’t follow easily. Basically a landscape connectivity experiment in 1958.
Before this, spatial concepts were essentially absent from coexistence theory. ,,,
Worth describing the apparatus: oranges as prey habitat, rubber balls as non-habitat, petroleum jelly barriers to slow the predator, and small wooden posts with wires so the prey mite — which disperses on silk threads — could travel while the walking predator could not.
Huffaker engineered a dispersal asymmetry. That is the mechanism, and it is the same mechanism that keeps metapopulations going: prey stay one step ahead in space, not in time.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Diffusion-reaction: Skellam 1951

Animal populations move in a very similar way.



Imagine a glass of water. If I add a drop of ink to water, I will see that the ink slowly spreads throughout the water on its own. The ink particles move from an area of high concentration to lower concentration, gradually mixing with water until it spreads evenly.
John Skellam was the first to realize that animal populations move in a very similar way, using a concept called reaction-diffusion.
Main point: Skellam proved that for a population to survive in a specific habitat patch, the patch must be large enough for the animals to reproduce faster than they “leak” out the edges. If the patch is too small, the “ink” (the population) spreads too thin and disappears.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Muskrat escape

Speed of invasion is determined by how fast individuals wander, and how fast they breed.



This is a map of central Europe. This is Prague in Czech Republic. In 1905, a handful of muskrats escaped a fur-breeding estate near Prague. Within two decades they were all over central Europe, and because they were a nuisance, the invasion was mapped carefully year by year. Skellam plotted the square root of the occupied area against time and got a straight line. Skellam used partial differential equations to track the “random walk” of organisms.
He modeled the speed of an invasion with two numbers. once you have these, you can forecast a biological invasion. Nobody had been able to do that before.
This laid the foundation for the Spatially Implicit Models (SIMs) we use to predict the spread of invasive species and the minimum area needed for nature reserves.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Herbivorous insects: Kareiva 1992

The diffusion coefficient is not a property of the organim: rather a property of the organism in a particular landscape.



Skellam gave us the math, he came up with a mathematical model to forcast invasion. The awkward part is that his equations contain a diffusion coefficient for how fast organisms wander. For decades, nobody measured it in the field. Like you have a reciepe book, that lists the ingredients but not their quantities!
With a 30 year gap, Kareiva did an experiment that brought that theoretical model to reality.
Kareiva is famous for bridging the gap between theoretical models and natural history. He conducted landmark experiments (often using ladybugs and aphids) to see if predators actually follow the “smooth” rules of movement Skellam predicted.
set up experimental collard arrays where he manipulated plant spacing and plant quality, marked Phyllotreta cruciferae beetles, released them, and tracked how they redistributed — then fit diffusion models to the results. The finding that mattered: the diffusion coefficient is not a property of the beetle. It’s a property of the beetle in a particular landscape. Change the spacing of the plants and you change how the animal moves through them.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Herbivorous insects: Kareiva 1993
Kareiva’s empirical test: diffusion models predicted spread adequately despite obviously non-random insect movement.


In A second study, Kareiva collected mark-recapture data for twelve species of herbivorous insects in relatively homogeneous habitats and asked whether a simple passive diffusion model could reproduce their dispersal-distance distributions. For eight of the twelve, it could.
The four that departed were the interesting ones — he treated the mismatches as instructions for how movement models needed to be modified, and noted that the variation in diffusion coefficients within and between species was large enough to have real consequences for population dynamics.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Activity overview

Format: small groups of 2–3
Materials: one printed 10 × 10 grid per group, pens
Every group gets an identical landscape: a 10 × 10 grid, 100 cells. Every group gets exactly 25 cells of habitat to shade in.
Your group’s job: arrange those 25 cells to give your species the best possible chance of persisting for 100 years. Shade them however you like.

Before you start, draw one card from the card deck. It tells you which species you are planning for. Do not show it to the other groups.

Preparation: print grids and cut two kinds of cards, roughly half and half.
CARD A — “Your species is a poor disperser. Adults rarely move more than one cell in a lifetime.”
CARD B — “Your species is a strong disperser but needs a large territory. A single pair requires at least 8 connected cells.”
That hidden asymmetry is the whole trick. Do not hint at it. Groups will assume everyone got the same brief, which is exactly what makes the reveal work.
Circulate while they draw. You will see three recurring solutions: one big block, a scatter of singletons, and a chain of clumps. All three are useful in the debrief.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Activity

Design (<4 min). Shade your 25 cells. Agree on your reasoning in one sentence.
Gallery walk (<6 min). Tape your grid to the wall. Walk the room. Do not talk yet, just look.
Two questions, whole class (<10 min).

Every landscape on this wall has exactly the same amount of habitat. Why do they look different?
Point to the grid you think is worst. Now find out which card that group drew.



The reveal is question 2. A design that is disastrous for Card A (scattered singletons, no cell adjacent to another) is often perfectly reasonable for Card B, and the block design that looks obviously right to Card B groups may strand a Card A population that cannot recolonise after a local die-off.
The line to land, in these words or close to them: the amount of habitat did not change — only its arrangement did — and the arrangement changed the answer. That sentence is the thesis of the entire course, and you have got students to generate it themselves in eight minutes rather than reading it in a preface.
If a group asks “what counts as connected?” — refuse to answer. Tell them to define it and write the definition on their grid. You will use those competing definitions again in Chapter 9.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Activity debrief
Without being told any of the terminology, your group made decisions about:

Patch size and isolation (the two axes of island biogeography theory)
Connectivity (whether an individual can get from A to B)
Species-specific perception of the same physical landscape
Configuration (arrangement versus amount)

You also discovered the uncomfortable part: the “right” map depends on the organism, and two competent groups looking at identical data can reach opposite conclusions when the organism differs.

Students arrive expecting spatial analysis to be a machine that produces the objectively correct map. It is not. It produces a map that is conditional on assumptions about the organism, and the whole discipline is about making those assumptions explicit and testable rather than tacit.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Island biogeography: MacArthur & Wilson

Patch size and spatial configuration govern persistence through colonization and extinction.



Area → extinction rate (bigger islands, smaller extinction risk)
Isolation → colonisation rate (nearer islands, higher colonisation)


Groups traded off patch size against isolation with 25 cells. That is the theory
If your individuals are allowed to disperse from a mainland source to sourranding islands: islands closer to the mainland have a higher colonization rate bigger islands have a smaller extinction risk.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
From islands to metapopulations

Dispersal can protect a local population from extinction.


How to model metapopulation dynamics?
➢ each patch can be occupied (1) or unoccupied (0)
➢ at each time step, occupied patches go extinct with probability ε
➢ unoccupied patches can be colonized with probability γ
➢ objective is to estimate the fraction of patches occupied ѱ



Dispersal … . This is a schematic of our metapop. Some sites are occupied, some aren’t. At each timestep, occupied patches go extinct with a probability…

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Metapopulation dynamic: Levins 1969

More patches leads to lower metapopulation extinction risk

✓ Unoccupied sites are “rescued” by colonization from occupied sites
✓ Critical to maintain patches, even if they are currently unoccupied
✓ Connectivity of patches important for increasing colonization probability

If there are more patches in a metapop, then the extinction risk will be lower. …
At any point in time, what proportion of sites will go extinct?
At any point in time, what proportion of sites will be colonized?
At any point in time, what proportion of sites will be occupied?
Levins 1969 is a two-page paper in a newsletter of the Entomological Society of America.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
What made it possible
The emergence of spatial modelling frameworks was fostered by technological advance at least as much as by theory:

Massive increases in high-resolution spatial data (e.g., GPS telemetry, LIDAR, remote sensing)
Advanced statistical methods (e.g., Geostatistics, Species Distribution Models, Individual Based Models)
Computing power
Open-source software ecosystems, which allow reproducible script-based modelling

These allowed conceptual and modelling developments to represent space more realistically. The ability to explicitly include the effects of space was pivotal in the explosion of novel ecological questions over recent decades.

We talked about theories built to hold space but it’s worth emphasizing what actually made it possible to model the role of space was technological advances, including remote sensing and computing power.
Watt had the idea of spatial patterns and processe in 1947. He could not have fitted a spatial regression to a Landsat data, because neither existed.
The bottleneck in this field has usually been measurement and computation, — which means that watching what becomes newly quantifiable is a reasonable strategy for finding research questions.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
How to incorporate space







Spatial aspect
Effect on process and data




x–y coordinates
Locations of data relative to other locations


autocorrelation
Magnitude, scale, direction of data as a function of distance between observations


relationship
Locations of abiotic predictor affect biotic response


legacy
Past spatial pattern influences present process and pattern


contingency
Nearby locations influence process and pattern


perception
Intervening landscape features shape movement and dispersal ability


multiple scales
Several scales act additively on present spatial pattern




Here is an overview of different ways space palys a role and can be incorporated in ecological data analysis. Think about your own research projects and pick the row most relevant to your work. It surfaces their systems early and gives you material for later examples.
Spatial perception is what we discovered in the second activity: the same physical landscape is a different landscape to a poor disperser and a strong one.
Your groups drew grids under two different dispersal assumptions and got two different “correct” answers. That is spatial perception.
Spatial legacy remember card 6? Neighbouring stands share an age class because one 1910 fire burned them together.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
What Is Randomness?

Every element has an equal and independent chance of being selected.
We cannot predict any single outcome with certainty — this is a random (stochastic) process.
Humans are poor random number generators. Ask ten people for “30 random points” and you will get suspiciously even spacing. That is why we use algorithms.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Uniform Distribution
Start with 100 draws from a uniform distribution between 0 and 10.

x_unif <- runif(n = 100, min = 0, max = 10)

summary(x_unif)
plot(x_unif, type = "h", col = "#333333",
     xlab = "Draw number", ylab = "Value",
     main = "100 uniform draws in the order sampled")


Compare your output with your neighbour’s. Did you get the same values?

Reproducibility with set.seed()

set.seed(2026)
a <- runif(5, 0, 10)

set.seed(2026)
b <- runif(5, 0, 10)

round(a, 4)
round(b, 4)
identical(a, b)







Note


set.seed() fixes the starting point of the random number generator. Put it at the top of any script you want to be reproducible.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Visualising the Distribution

set.seed(2026)
x_unif <- runif(n = 100, min = 0, max = 10)

hist(x_unif,
     col    = "#DFD1A7",
     border = "#333333",
     xlab   = "Value",
     main   = "Uniform(0, 10), n = 100")

The bars are roughly level across the range because every value between 0 and 10 is equally likely. With only 100 draws the sampling noise is still obvious.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Sample Size and Shape







Exercise 3


Run the code, then change the four sample sizes and re-run. How does the histogram shape change as n grows?





set.seed(2026)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

for (n in c(50, 250, 500, 5000)) {
  x <- runif(n = n, min = 0, max = 10)
  hist(x, main = paste("n =", n), xlab = "Value",
       col = "#DFD1A7", border = "#333333")
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))








Solution


set.seed(2026)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (n in c(50, 250, 500, 5000)) {
  x <- runif(n = n, min = 0, max = 10)
  hist(x, main = paste("n =", n), xlab = "Value",
       col = "#DFD1A7", border = "#333333")
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
As n grows the bars flatten out toward the true uniform density. Small samples look lumpy purely by chance — a useful reminder when you interpret a histogram of 30 field measurements.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Normal Distribution
rnorm() takes a sample size, a mean, and a standard deviation.

set.seed(2026)
x_norm <- rnorm(n = 100, mean = 0, sd = 1)

summary(x_norm)
round(c(mean = mean(x_norm), sd = sd(x_norm)), 3)


Are the sample mean and standard deviation exactly 0 and 1? Why not?

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Density, Mean, and Interval

set.seed(2026)
x_norm <- rnorm(n = 100, mean = 0, sd = 1)

plot(density(x_norm),
     lwd = 3,
     col = "#333333",
     main = "Normal(0, 1),
     n = 100",
     xlab = "Value")

abline(v = mean(x_norm), lwd = 3, col = "#70002E")

ci <- quantile(x_norm, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
abline(v = ci, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "#70002E")

legend("topright",
       bty = "n",
       legend = c("Density", "Mean", "95% interval"),
       col = c("#333333", "#70002E", "#70002E"),
       lty = c(1, 1, 2),
       lwd = c(3, 3, 2))

The solid maroon line marks the sample mean near zero; the dashed lines mark the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles, roughly symmetric around it.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Histogram and Density Together

set.seed(2026)
x_norm <- rnorm(n = 100, mean = 0, sd = 1)

hist(x_norm, 
     probability = TRUE,
     col = "#EFE8D4",
     border = "#333333",
     xlab = "Value", 
     main = "")
lines(density(x_norm), col = "#70002E", lwd = 4)







Note


probability = TRUE plots density rather than frequency, so the histogram and the smooth curve share a vertical scale. With probability = FALSE (the default) the curve would be flat against the axis.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Comparing Two Distributions

set.seed(2026)
x1 <- rnorm(1000, mean = 25, sd = 5)   # adults
x2 <- rnorm(1000, mean = 15, sd = 2)   # juveniles

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

plot(density(x1),
     col = "#70002E",
     lwd = 4,
     lty = 1,
     xlim = c(5, 45), 
     ylim = c(0, 0.30),
     main = "Kernel densities", 
     xlab = "Mass (kg)")
lines(density(x2), col = "#1D3C34", lwd = 4, lty = 2)
legend("topright",
       bty = "n",
       legend = c("Adult", "Juvenile"),
       col = c("#70002E", "#1D3C34"),
       lty = c(1, 2),
       lwd = 4)

mass <- rbind(data.frame(x = x1, stage = "Adult"),
              data.frame(x = x2, stage = "Juvenile"))
boxplot(x ~ stage, 
        data = mass, 
        col = c("#DFD1A7", "#BBDDE6"),
        ylab = "Mass (kg)",
        xlab = "",
        main = "Box-and-whisker")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Adults centre near 25 kg with a wide spread; juveniles centre near 15 kg and are much tighter. Line type distinguishes the two curves as well as colour.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Poisson Distribution
Count data are often modelled as Poisson. It has a single parameter, the mean count λ (lambda).

set.seed(2026)
x_pois <- rpois(n = 250, lambda = 3.3)

table(x_pois)
hist(x_pois, 
     probability = TRUE,
     breaks = seq(-0.5, max(x_pois) + 0.5, 1),
     col = "#DFD1A7",
     border = "#333333",
     xlab = "Count", 
     main = "Poisson(lambda = 3.3)")







Note


For a Poisson, the variance equals the mean. Real count data are often overdispersed, i.e., more variable and that is when negative binomial models are useful.

Your Turn: Three Values of Lambda







Exercise 4


Run the code, then change the three values of λ. At what point does the distribution stop looking skewed?

par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

for (m in c(1, 5, 15)) {
  x <- rpois(250, lambda = m)
  hist(x, 
       main = paste("lambda =", m),
       xlab = "Count",
       probability = TRUE,
       col = "#DFD1A7",
       border = "#333333")
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))








Solution


set.seed(2026)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (m in c(1, 5, 15)) {
  x <- rpois(250, lambda = m)
  hist(x, 
  main = paste("lambda =", m),
  xlab = "Count",
  probability = TRUE, 
  col = "#DFD1A7", 
  border = "#333333")
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
At λ = 1 the distribution is strongly right-skewed and piles up at zero. By λ = 15 it is nearly symmetric — Poisson approaches normal as λ grows.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Binomial and Bernoulli
The binomial arises when repeated trials have binary outcome. rbinom() takes the number of observations, trials per observation, and probability of success.

set.seed(2026)

# 10 observations, each of 5 trials, p = 0.25
x_binom <- rbinom(n = 10, size = 5, prob = 0.25)
x_binom

# Bernoulli: a single trial per observation
x_bern <- rbinom(n = 20, size = 1, prob = 0.35)
x_bern

barplot(table(factor(x_bern, levels = c(0, 1),
                     labels = c("Failure", "Success"))),
        col = c("#DFD1A7", "#70002E"),
        xlab = "Outcome", ylab = "Number of cases")







Note


This is the detection process behind occupancy models: each camera visit is a Bernoulli trial with detection probability p, and the number of visits with a detection out of K visits is binomial.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Base Plotting Functions

plot(x, y) : scatter, line, or formula plots
hist(x) : distribution of one variable
boxplot(y ~ group) : distribution across groups
barplot(height) : tallies and totals
pairs(df) : all pairwise scatterplots, for spotting collinearity among predictors

Add-on packages include ggplot2 and lattice. We use base graphics here because terra and sf both plug straight into it.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
A First Plot

set.seed(591)
sp  <- c("Elk", "Mule Deer", "Black Bear", "Steller's Jay", "Clark's Nutcracker")
cls <- c("Mammal", "Mammal", "Mammal", "Bird", "Bird")
camera <- expand.grid(site_id = sprintf("S%02d", 1:20),
                      week = 1:8,
                      species = sp,
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
camera$class <- cls[match(camera$species, sp)]
camera$count <- rpois(nrow(camera),
                      lambda = ifelse(camera$class == "Bird", 2.5, 1.2))
wk <- aggregate(count ~ week, data = camera, FUN = sum)
wk

plot(count ~ week, data = wk)

The default plot is functional but can be customized, shown next.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Controlling the Plot

wk <- aggregate(count ~ week, data = camera, FUN = sum)

plot(count ~ week,
     data = wk,
     type  = "l", lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#767676",
     axes  = FALSE, frame = FALSE,
     xlim  = c(0.5, 8.5),
     ylim  = c(0, max(wk$count) + 40),
     xaxs  = "i", yaxs = "i",
     xlab  = "Survey week",
     ylab  = "Total detections")

axis(1, at = 1:8, labels = 1:8, las = 1, lwd = 2)
axis(2, at = seq(0, max(wk$count) + 40, 40), las = 1, lwd = 2)

points(count ~ week, data = wk, pch = 19, cex = 1.4, col = "#70002E")

Detections stay roughly the same across the eight weeks, as they should. The simulation used the same λ every week.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Two Groups on One Plot

wk_cls <- aggregate(count ~ week + class, data = camera, FUN = sum)

mam <- wk_cls[wk_cls$class == "Mammal", ]
avs <- wk_cls[wk_cls$class == "Bird", ]

plot(count ~ week, data = mam,
     pch = 19, cex = 1.5, col = "#70002E", type = "b", lwd = 2, lty = 1,
     ylim = c(0, max(wk_cls$count) + 20),
     xlab = "Survey week", ylab = "Total detections")

points(count ~ week, data = avs,
       pch = 17, cex = 1.5, col = "#1D3C34", type = "b", lwd = 2, lty = 2)

legend("topright", bty = "n",
       legend = c("Mammals", "Birds"),
       pch = c(19, 17), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2,
       col = c("#70002E", "#1D3C34"))








Design note


The two series differ by colour, point shape, and line type. Redundant encoding keeps the figure readable in greyscale and for colour-blind readers.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Bar Plots of Totals

tot <- tapply(camera$count, camera$species, sum)
tot <- sort(tot, decreasing = TRUE)

par(mar = c(9, 5, 2, 1))
barplot(tot,
        col       = "#70002E",
        density   = seq(20, 60, length.out = length(tot)),
        ylab      = "Total detections",
        las       = 2,
        cex.names = 0.9)
par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Small Multiples

sp_list <- unique(camera$species)
wk_sp   <- aggregate(count ~ week + species, data = camera, FUN = sum)

par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

for (s in sp_list) {
  d <- wk_sp[wk_sp$species == s, ]
  plot(count ~ week, data = d,
       type = "h", lwd = 8, lend = 1, col = "#1D3C34",
       ylim = c(0, max(wk_sp$count)),
       main = s, cex.main = 0.95,
       xlab = "Week", ylab = "Detections")
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)

Shared axis limits across panels are what make small multiples comparable. Drop ylim and each panel rescales, which hides the real differences between species.
